taxonomyNote: NatureServe notes Brandley et al. (2010) found multiple lineages within N. rhombifer (east and west of the Mississippi River, plus Mexico); treated here as one species.
fieldMarks: Large, heavy-bodied watersnake; adults usually 3-5 ft (Missouri: 30-48 in, occasionally to 69 in).
Dark brown blotches along the back usually connect into a chainlike pattern, with light diamond-shaped areas between; dark bars on the sides alternate to form diamonds.
Belly yellow with irregular rows of dark spots or half-moon marks.
Scales keeled, so the snake feels rough.
behavior: Diurnal in spring and fall and nocturnal in summer; bask on branches, logs and banks except in the hottest weather.
Eats mainly fishes and frogs, also salamanders, carrion and small turtles; feeds by day.
Overwinters underground below the frost line, including in crayfish burrows; bites hard and musks when handled.
habitat: Margins and shallows of lakes, ponds, rivers, streams, swamps, marshes, canals and ditches; most common in swamps, sloughs, oxbows and drainage ditches in Missouri.
range: Concentrated in the Mississippi River drainage, north to southern Illinois and Indiana, west to Texas and Oklahoma (and Mexico), east into Alabama. Not in Canada.

lookalikes.name: Northern cottonmouth
lookalikes.howToTell: Cottonmouth has a distinctly triangular head, a sensory pit between nostril and eye, a light line from eye to mouth corner, and no chainlike dark back pattern.
